# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Phase 1 — Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug — one that goes red on _this_ bug — you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one — try them in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug — unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.

4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.
"}

name: using-git-worktrees
description: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - creates isolated git worktrees with smart directory selection and safety verification
---

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

## Safety Verification

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory is ignored (respects local, global, and system gitignore)
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check CLAUDE.md → Ask user |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

### Skipping ignore verification

- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask

### Proceeding with failing tests

- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

### Hardcoding setup commands

- **Problem:** Breaks on projects using different tools
- **Fix:** Auto-detect from project files (package.json, etc.)

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace.

[Check .worktrees/ - exists]
[Verify ignored - git check-ignore confirms .worktrees/ is ignored]
[Create worktree: git worktree add .worktrees/auth -b feature/auth]
[Run npm install]
[Run npm test - 47 passing]

Worktree ready at /Users/jesse/myproject/.worktrees/auth
Tests passing (47 tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement auth feature
```

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Create worktree without verifying it's ignored (project-local)
- Skip baseline test verification
- Proceed with failing tests without asking
- Assume directory location when ambiguous
- Skip CLAUDE.md check

**Always:**
- Follow directory priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask
- Verify directory is ignored for project-local
- Auto-detect and run project setup
- Verify clean test baseline

## Integration

**Called by:**
- **brainstorming** (Phase 4) - REQUIRED when design is approved and implementation follows
- **subagent-driven-development** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- **executing-plans** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- Any skill needing isolated workspace

**Pairs with:**
- **finishing-a-development-branch** - REQUIRED for cleanup after work complete
# Module Ownership and Reuse

This is the implementation ownership map for maintaining Mesh Talk and assigning
parallel work. Use it to locate the owner of a decision before adding another
implementation. Network semantics and configuration belong to the
[communication architecture](network-design-reference.md); this document defines
where those decisions live in code and how to change them safely.

The [canonical glossary](../CONTEXT.md) defines domain concepts;
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) define modeling terms and identifier mappings.
The layers and owners below are implementation responsibilities, not declarations
that every module or crate is a separate DDD bounded context.

## 1. Dependency direction

| Layer                                       | Owns                                                                                          | Depends on                                              | Must delegate                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Protocol core: `crates/mesh-talk-core`      | Identity, membership, encryption, admission, persistence, transport and delivery correctness  | Rust libraries and its internal modules                 | Native platform behavior and presentation                            |
| Desktop host: `src-tauri`                   | Session/runtime installation, OS integration, settings persistence, authorized IPC adaptation | Core public exports                                     | Wire validation, cryptographic authority and delivery state machines |
| Typed IPC: `frontend/src/lib/api`           | Command names, payload shapes, typed results                                                  | Shared types, Tauri APIs and sibling adapters           | UI stores, React features and business decisions                     |
| Application stores: `frontend/src/store`    | Reactive state, owner-scoped work, optimistic intents, cache transitions                      | Typed adapters and shared projections                   | Core authority and feature rendering                                 |
| Feature modules: `frontend/src/features`    | User interaction and composition                                                              | Stores, typed adapters, shared models and UI primitives | Reimplementation of identity, policy or delivery rules               |
| UI primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui` | Accessible visual controls                                                                    | React/Radix and styling helpers                         | Session lifecycle and protocol policy                                |

The bot integration service in `crates/mesh-talk-integrations` depends on the core
and host-supplied admission ports. It owns grants, bounded metadata audit and
private IPC and its fixed-route loopback HTTP adapter; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp` owns SDK/stdio translation only. Core
`node/outgoing_message.rs` owns retry-safe event acceptance and sender-state WAL
recovery. Desktop `src-tauri/src/integrations.rs` binds exact-session leases and
graceful listener retirement. `integrations/local_access.rs` owns serialized
settings/startup control and the single desktop service handle;
`integrations/instructions.rs` owns only the marked user-level bootstrap file.
Both transports share one integration service/registry and core sending path.
`http.rs` owns public static discovery, request limits and fixed scoped routes;
request schemas derive from the existing models. The Agent access settings UI uses
the shared save coordinator and an explicit-owner typed adapter. See
[desktop local access](bot-integrations.md#desktop-local-agent-access).

The local access owner persists absolute authorization deadlines and preserves
them across service retries and session/runtime restarts. Only an explicitly
verified enable, duration extension or renewal can extend authority. The shared
integration grant authorizer checks expiry again at core acceptance. The desktop
activity view uses the existing registry's bounded content-free send projection:
read the live service registry while its supervisor exists, and open the saved
registry only after its writer has stopped under the same controller serialization.
The UI never creates a second grant-store owner or attributes a shared credential
to a particular AI application. See [authorization lifetime](bot-integrations.md#lifecycle-and-authority).

The headless CLI uses the core directly. A protocol change should not require
Tauri; a presentation change should not alter the wire protocol. Not every helper
in `lib/` is pure: `theme.ts`, for example, owns reactive appearance effects. Use
specific modules rather than assuming the directory name implies purity.

The existing API facade remains stable. Its settings owner resolver is composed
at the application seam; adapters never import stores. ESLint enforces that rule
for alias imports and relative imports at any nesting depth. The auth store uses
low-level adapters to avoid recreating the facade/settings/auth runtime cycle.

ESLint also rejects static imports of rendering modules (`components/` and
`features/`) from stores and IPC adapters, including type-only imports and nested
relative paths. Shared presence vocabulary lives in `lib/presence.ts`; identity
controls re-export it for compatibility. Stores own evidence expiry and state
transitions; controls own visual mapping. These checks cover direct static
dependencies, not transitive dependencies or dynamic imports.

## 2. Feature owners and shared decisions

Paths below are relative to the repository root. `core/` abbreviates
`crates/mesh-talk-core/src/`; `ui/` abbreviates `frontend/src/`.

These owners already exist. Adding a new abstraction is justified by a shared

example, discovery TTL and conversation presence need not share a constant just

# Mesh-Talk domain language

Mesh-Talk supports private conversations between authenticated participants across
local and existing routed networks, with optional peer-operated encrypted custody.
This is the canonical glossary; [DDD conventions](docs/domain-design.md) own its
use in code, ownership decisions and documentation.

## Identity and access

**Local user**:
A local sign-in identity and its protected application data. A local user is not
the cross-device mesh account or a network device.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID when referring to the local login identity.

**Username / account login name**:
The name entered at sign-in. Linked desktop devices use the kept account's same
login name and password. It is distinct from the account nickname and from the
immutable local storage username retained internally for an existing local user.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID, nickname, storage directory as interchangeable names.

**Local storage username**:
The existing per-device storage namespace for a local user. Account login
migration preserves this name and the local-user UUID; a credential envelope maps
the shared login to the retained local owner and its separate storage secrets.
_Avoid_: account login name, account ID, shared password.

**Display name**:
A human-readable label for presentation. It is neither unique identity nor
proof of authority.
_Avoid_: identifier, verified identity.

**Account**:
A cryptographic identity shared across certified devices. Account identity does
not depend on a desktop login, IP address or display name.
_Avoid_: local user, machine, device.

**Account profile**:
Account-authenticated nickname, biography and avatar, saved through ordinary
profile editing and synchronized automatically. It carries read-only creation
metadata when known; revisions order updates across devices.
_Avoid_: local login profile, device identity, proof of a person's identity.

Linked devices share account login credentials through private account access. Login names remain distinct from public nicknames; device identities and local encrypted-storage secrets remain distinct.

**Device**:
A participant identified by its persistent signing and key-agreement identity.
Restarting a process does not by itself create a new device.
_Avoid_: running instance, account, physical computer.

**Device certificate**:
An account-signed binding of a device's public identity to that account.
_Avoid_: discovery record, membership grant.

**Account group role**:
The account's accepted member or owner role in a channel. Certified devices
present the same account role. The public membership state and verified account
bindings establish that role; device reachability determines execution
availability, not a different role. Legacy public controls retain their existing
signer requirements.
_Avoid_: online status, device approval, shared group reference.

**Account group operation**:
An account-authorized intent to change channel state or send channel content.
Its pending identity is distinct from the public events that commit its effects.
Execution may use an authorized device without changing the account's role or
reattributing existing public events.
_Avoid_: committed event before acceptance, device-specific permission.

**Peer**:
Another known network device, including an infrastructure device when the role
permits it. A peer is not necessarily a person or a channel member.
_Avoid_: user, contact, member as interchangeable names.

**Contact**:
An account represented in local conversation/contact state. Contact visibility
is separate from discovery, delivery permission and channel membership.
_Avoid_: online peer, accepted member.

**Desktop session**:
One authenticated local user's login lifetime. A subsequent login starts a new
lifetime even when it belongs to the same local user.
_Avoid_: transport session, ratchet session, account lifetime.

**Participant runtime**:
The active network-participation lifetime of an initialized node. It is distinct
from persistent device identity and the host's login lifetime.
_Avoid_: device, desktop session.

**Integration grant**:
An authorization for a local client to perform specified integration operations
for permitted destinations within its validity period.
_Avoid_: channel membership, device certificate, session token.

## Conversations and history

**Personal conversation removal**:
An account-private decision to remove a chat, optionally erasing its history on
certified linked devices. Durable deletion floors prevent stale private replay;
each device confirms its own cleanup separately. It is distinct from leaving or
dissolving a group, recalling a message and blocking a contact.

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

## Safety Verification

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory is ignored (respects local, global, and system gitignore)
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check CLAUDE.md → Ask user |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

### Skipping ignore verification

- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask

### Proceeding with failing tests

- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

### Hardcoding setup commands

- **Problem:** Breaks on projects using different tools
- **Fix:** Auto-detect from project files (package.json, etc.)

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace.

[Check .worktrees/ - exists]
[Verify ignored - git check-ignore confirms .worktrees/ is ignored]
[Create worktree: git worktree add .worktrees/auth -b feature/auth]
[Run npm install]
[Run npm test - 47 passing]

Worktree ready at /Users/jesse/myproject/.worktrees/auth
Tests passing (47 tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement auth feature
```

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Create worktree without verifying it's ignored (project-local)
- Skip baseline test verification
- Proceed with failing tests without asking
- Assume directory location when ambiguous
- Skip CLAUDE.md check

**Always:**
- Follow directory priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask
- Verify directory is ignored for project-local
- Auto-detect and run project setup
- Verify clean test baseline

## Integration

**Called by:**
- **brainstorming** (Phase 4) - REQUIRED when design is approved and implementation follows
- **subagent-driven-development** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- **executing-plans** - REQUIRED before executing any tasks
- Any skill needing isolated workspace

**Pairs with:**
- **finishing-a-development-branch** - REQUIRED for cleanup after work complete

where those decisions live in code and how to change them safely.

The [canonical glossary](../CONTEXT.md) defines domain concepts;
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) define modeling terms and identifier mappings.
The layers and owners below are implementation responsibilities, not declarations
that every module or crate is a separate DDD bounded context.

pixels and decoder allocation at most 64 MiB; this is not a whole-process budget.
APNG retains its original animation, and GIF/WebP/video keep their existing paths.
Current protection, expiry, consent and source identity are rechecked around work.

# Mesh-Talk domain language

Mesh-Talk supports private conversations between authenticated participants across
local and existing routed networks, with optional peer-operated encrypted custody.
This is the canonical glossary; [DDD conventions](docs/domain-design.md) own its
use in code, ownership decisions and documentation.

## Identity and access

**Local user**:
A local sign-in identity and its protected application data. A local user is not
the cross-device mesh account or a network device.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID when referring to the local login identity.

**Username / account login name**:
The name entered at sign-in. Linked desktop devices use the kept account's same
login name and password. It is distinct from the account nickname and from the
immutable local storage username retained internally for an existing local user.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID, nickname, storage directory as interchangeable names.

**Local storage username**:
The existing per-device storage namespace for a local user. Account login
migration preserves this name and the local-user UUID; a credential envelope maps
the shared login to the retained local owner and its separate storage secrets.
_Avoid_: account login name, account ID, shared password.

**Display name**:
A human-readable label for presentation. It is neither unique identity nor
proof of authority.
_Avoid_: identifier, verified identity.

**Account**:
A cryptographic identity shared across certified devices. Account identity does
not depend on a desktop login, IP address or display name.
_Avoid_: local user, machine, device.

**Account profile**:
Account-authenticated nickname, biography and avatar, saved through ordinary
profile editing and synchronized automatically. It carries read-only creation
metadata when known; revisions order updates across devices.
_Avoid_: local login profile, device identity, proof of a person's identity.

Linked devices share account login credentials through private account access. Login names remain distinct from public nicknames; device identities and local encrypted-storage secrets remain distinct.

**Device**:
A participant identified by its persistent signing and key-agreement identity.
Restarting a process does not by itself create a new device.
_Avoid_: running instance, account, physical computer.

**Device certificate**:
An account-signed binding of a device's public identity to that account.
_Avoid_: discovery record, membership grant.

**Account group role**:
The account's accepted member or owner role in a channel. Certified devices
present the same account role. The public membership state and verified account
bindings establish that role; device reachability determines execution
availability, not a different role. Legacy public controls retain their existing
signer requirements.
_Avoid_: online status, device approval, shared group reference.

**Account group operation**:
An account-authorized intent to change channel state or send channel content.
Its pending identity is distinct from the public events that commit its effects.
Execution may use an authorized device without changing the account's role or
reattributing existing public events.
_Avoid_: committed event before acceptance, device-specific permission.

**Peer**:
Another known network device, including an infrastructure device when the role
permits it. A peer is not necessarily a person or a channel member.
_Avoid_: user, contact, member as interchangeable names.

**Contact**:
An account represented in local conversation/contact state. Contact visibility
is separate from discovery, delivery permission and channel membership.
_Avoid_: online peer, accepted member.

**Desktop session**:
One authenticated local user's login lifetime. A subsequent login starts a new
lifetime even when it belongs to the same local user.
_Avoid_: transport session, ratchet session, account lifetime.

**Participant runtime**:
The active network-participation lifetime of an initialized node. It is distinct
from persistent device identity and the host's login lifetime.
_Avoid_: device, desktop session.

**Integration grant**:
An authorization for a local client to perform specified integration operations
for permitted destinations within its validity period.
_Avoid_: channel membership, device certificate, session token.

## Conversations and history

**Personal conversation removal**:
An account-private decision to remove a chat, optionally erasing its history on
certified linked devices. Durable deletion floors prevent stale private replay;
each device confirms its own cleanup separately. It is distinct from leaving or
dissolving a group, recalling a message and blocking a contact.

# Mesh-Talk Architecture

A decentralized, end-to-end-encrypted messenger. **Tauri** desktop shell, **Rust**
backend, **React + TypeScript** frontend. No vendor-operated server: LAN peers
discover each other over signed UDP **multicast** (group `224.0.0.167`, port
47474), connect directly over a Noise-encrypted TCP
channel, and store messages as an append-only, hash-linked **event log** that syncs CRDT-style.
When a peer is offline, a peer-operated **post office** node stores-and-forwards the (still-encrypted)
events. Existing routed networks can supply optional peer discovery; opted-in
post-office bridges introduce registered peers across sites without merging
their IP subnets. See [routed discovery](routed-network-discovery.md) and
[Network Topology and Communication Architecture](network-design-reference.md)
for cross-module design contracts, illustrated scenarios and development guardrails;
[network topologies](network-topologies.md) provides the compact overview.

> The earlier RSA-contact / plaintext-UDP / TCP-relay _legacy_ stack has been retired;
> this local-first stack is the entire product and lives at `/`. The only retained
> piece outside the node is the auth/session layer (`services/auth_service.rs` + `state.rs`),
> which `login` uses before starting the node.

---

Use the [canonical domain glossary](../CONTEXT.md) and
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) for terminology and identifier translations.
This reference owns technical mechanisms and invariants.

## 1. Process & layers

See the [module ownership and reuse guide](module-boundaries.md) before assigning
parallel feature work or adding shared business logic. It maps current owners and
feature-local interfaces across the core, desktop host and frontend.

```
React UI ── lib/api/*.ts ──invoke()──▶ Tauri IPC (chat_commands/)
   ▲                                    │
   │ Tauri events                       ▼
   └─────────────── RuntimeEvents ← NodeRuntime (node/runtime.rs)
                                           │ discovery, accept, maintenance
                                           ▼
                                   Node (node/node.rs) — orchestration
        ┌──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬───────┴──────┐
   identity/      transport/        eventlog/       discovery/    postoffice/
   ratchet/       (Noise XX)        (DAG + sync)    (signed UDP)  (elect+relay)
   channel/ dm/
        └────────────── storage/encryption.rs (PBKDF2-600k + AES-256-GCM at rest) ──┘
```

`mesh-talk-core` owns protocol state, network tasks, and encrypted persistence.
The desktop shell composes it using `RuntimeConfig` and `RuntimeEvents` in
`src-tauri/src/commands.rs`. `NodeRuntime::start` remains a compatibility
constructor for SDK callers. The shell owns the session and translates inbound
events to Tauri events; it does not own protocol or wire types. Desktop IPC
commands live in `src-tauri/src/chat_commands/`, grouped by account, messaging,
channels, files, platform, and diagnostics. `mod.rs` re-exports the established
command names for Tauri registration. Sensitive IPC commands capture `RuntimeAdmission` before waiting on `NodeState`.
Blocking operations retain runtime lifecycle and matching session authority until
completion, even when their IPC waiter is cancelled. Asynchronous producers use
guarded core commit seams; plaintext queries recheck the originating admission
before returning results. A cloned node handle alone conveys no session authority.
The installed runtime slot uses shared operation leases and exclusive replacement
access. Network waits in one producer must not serialize identity, presence,
history or unrelated sends. Retirement still waits for every admitted lease;
session authorization continues to enclose synchronous commits.

## 2. Crypto & identity (`identity/`, `transport/`, `ratchet/`, `dm/`, `channel/`)

### Protected messages

Text and image messages can carry an authenticated `MessageProtection` policy: explicit
click-to-view, or authentication with the viewing device's existing app-lock
mechanism. Core history, search and received-event projections omit protected
content; explicit exact-message text and image queries are available to authorized
hosts. Ordinary image read and export APIs reject protected images.
The encrypted sent/received stores and eligible history replication retain the
full protected body. Ordinary text/reply and sticker wire layouts stay unchanged.

Protected wire bodies reserve an outer `MTEX1` zero-deadline sentinel, followed
by an optional ordinary nonzero-deadline frame and the strict versioned `MTPR1`
body. Existing expiry-aware clients reject the outer zero sentinel before their
raw-text fallback. The body carries base64 text so even clients predating expiry
framing do not render literal message text through that fallback. This encoding
is not encryption or access authorization; existing DM/channel encryption remains
the confidentiality boundary. Unknown or malformed protected bodies fail closed.
Updated clients preserve the nested absolute expiry independently of the
30-second local reveal. Older clients cannot reveal protected messages and may
display an empty or encoded item; there is no automatic ordinary-text downgrade.

Protected images wrap an existing encrypted file manifest in a strict versioned
`MFP1` protection envelope. Ordinary file manifests remain byte-compatible; older
clients cannot decode the protected wrapper and do not receive an ordinary image
downgrade. File chunks, integrity checks, transfer consent and encrypted media
persistence keep their existing owners. The canonical file binding retains the
protection requirement, so another filename or offer cannot grant ordinary access
to the same protected transfer. The explicit image reveal resolves the retained
message reference before reading image bytes. Ordinary media reads require a known
unprotected manifest; retiring metadata before blob cleanup cannot grant access.
Channel image admission retains the manifest and protection policy in the existing
delivery WAL. Recovery projects manifest history and retained chunk scope before
retiring the transaction; projection failure preserves the accepted message ID
instead of reporting a new send failure.

The desktop reveal command captures `RuntimeAdmission`, validates an exact
account/channel message reference, and reuses the app-lock credential verifier
when required. It checks the same desktop session, installed participant runtime,
lock state and retained message again after authentication. Recall, expiry,
logout or runtime replacement during the prompt prevents content publication.
The verifier does not unlock the app and its result is not shared across messages.

The frontend keeps the returned body in temporary message-view state for at most
30 seconds and clears it when the view, conversation or owner retires, or the app
loses focus or visibility. Late IPC results cannot restore a retired reveal.
Image previews use component-local Blob URLs, revoked when concealed or retired,
and never use the ordinary shared image URL cache.
Ordinary history IPC, accessibility summaries, notifications, conversation
previews and reply quotes carry placeholders. This is a supported-client
presentation control, separate from encryption at rest, message expiry and
retention; it cannot prevent a recipient from modifying their client or capturing
already displayed content. See [protected-message behavior](privacy-controls.md#protected-messages).

### Fixed-deadline messages

The composer optionally selects a per-message duration and computes
one UTC expiry timestamp at send time. The timestamp is inside authenticated DM,
channel, or file-manifest plaintext (`MTEX1` frame), so every recipient device
receives the same deadline. Both sender and recipient history and search exclude
expired content; incoming notifications exclude expired arrivals. History IPC
returns the authenticated deadline for per-message countdowns. A single desktop
session monotonic clock removes expired cached messages and outgoing intents and updates
countdowns without per-message IPC. Focus and visibility changes recheck deadlines;
the history dialog filters and clears its own expired rows.
A one-second core maintenance task removes plaintext sidecars on both sides,
cancels expired outgoing retry work, suppresses replay through account sync, and
removes locally managed media. Queries enforce deadlines independently of cleanup;
cleanup errors are logged and retried on the next maintenance pass. A monotonic
observation timer also bounds the lifetime by the sender event's intended duration if the local
wall clock was already wrong when the message arrived. On restart the prior monotonic
clock anchor cannot be recovered; expiring recipient copies are erased early to
avoid extending their lifetime after a backward clock change. This is a local
retention feature: a recipient who controls their device can copy content or
modify the client, so remote deletion cannot be guaranteed. Older clients do
not understand the `MTEX1` frame and may keep its decrypted bytes; only updated
devices enforce expiry. Delayed delivery never restarts the countdown, and
already-expired arrivals are hidden. Sender copies keep their deadline across
restart; conservative early deletion on restart applies to recipient copies only.

# Requesting Code Review

Dispatch superpowers:code-reviewer subagent to catch issues before they cascade. The reviewer gets precisely crafted context for evaluation — never your session's history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the work product, not your thought process, and preserves your own context for continued work.

**Core principle:** Review early, review often.

## When to Request Review

**Mandatory:**
- After each task in subagent-driven development
- After completing major feature
- Before merge to main

**Optional but valuable:**
- When stuck (fresh perspective)
- Before refactoring (baseline check)
- After fixing complex bug

## How to Request

**1. Get git SHAs:**
```bash
BASE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1)  # or origin/main
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

**2. Dispatch code-reviewer subagent:**

Use Task tool with superpowers:code-reviewer type, fill template at `code-reviewer.md`

**Placeholders:**
- `{WHAT_WAS_IMPLEMENTED}` - What you just built
- `{PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS}` - What it should do
- `{BASE_SHA}` - Starting commit
- `{HEAD_SHA}` - Ending commit
- `{DESCRIPTION}` - Brief summary

**3. Act on feedback:**
- Fix Critical issues immediately
- Fix Important issues before proceeding
- Note Minor issues for later
- Push back if reviewer is wrong (with reasoning)

## Example

```
[Just completed Task 2: Add verification function]

You: Let me request code review before proceeding.

BASE_SHA=$(git log --oneline | grep "Task 1" | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

[Dispatch superpowers:code-reviewer subagent]
  WHAT_WAS_IMPLEMENTED: Verification and repair functions for conversation index
  PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS: Task 2 from docs/superpowers/plans/deployment-plan.md
  BASE_SHA: a7981ec
  HEAD_SHA: 3df7661
  DESCRIPTION: Added verifyIndex() and repairIndex() with 4 issue types

[Subagent returns]:
  Strengths: Clean architecture, real tests
  Issues:
    Important: Missing progress indicators
    Minor: Magic number (100) for reporting interval
  Assessment: Ready to proceed

You: [Fix progress indicators]
[Continue to Task 3]
```

## Integration with Workflows

**Subagent-Driven Development:**
- Review after EACH task
- Catch issues before they compound
- Fix before moving to next task

**Executing Plans:**
- Review after each batch (3 tasks)
- Get feedback, apply, continue

**Ad-Hoc Development:**
- Review before merge
- Review when stuck

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Skip review because "it's simple"
- Ignore Critical issues
- Proceed with unfixed Important issues
- Argue with valid technical feedback

**If reviewer wrong:**
- Push back with technical reasoning
- Show code/tests that prove it works
- Request clarification

See template at: requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

description: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work - guides completion of development work by presenting structured options for merge, PR, or cleanup

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

Guide completion of development work by presenting clear options and handling chosen workflow.

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## The Process

### Step 1: Verify Tests

**Before presenting options, verify tests pass:**

```bash
# Run project's test suite
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:**
```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]

Cannot proceed with merge/PR until tests pass.
```

Stop. Don't proceed to Step 2.

**If tests pass:** Continue to Step 2.

### Step 2: Determine Base Branch

```bash
# Try common base branches
git merge-base HEAD main 2>/dev/null || git merge-base HEAD master 2>/dev/null
```

Or ask: "This branch split from main - is that correct?"

### Step 3: Present Options

Present exactly these 4 options:

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)
4. Discard this work

Which option?
```

**Don't add explanation** - keep options concise.

### Step 4: Execute Choice

#### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Switch to base branch
git checkout <base-branch>

# Pull latest
git pull

# Merge feature branch
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>

# If tests pass
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

#### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
# Push branch
git push -u origin <feature-branch>

# Create PR
gh pr create --title "<title>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<2-3 bullets of what changed>

## Test Plan
- [ ] <verification steps>
EOF
)"
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

#### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

**Don't cleanup worktree.**

#### Option 4: Discard

**Confirm first:**
```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for exact confirmation.

If confirmed:
```bash
git checkout <base-branch>
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

### Step 5: Cleanup Worktree

**For Options 1, 2, 4:**

Check if in worktree:
```bash
git worktree list | grep $(git branch --show-current)
```

If yes:
```bash
git worktree remove <worktree-path>
```

**For Option 3:** Keep worktree.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | ✓ | - | - | ✓ |
| 2. Create PR | - | ✓ | ✓ | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | ✓ | - |
| 4. Discard | - | - | - | ✓ (force) |

## Common Mistakes

**Skipping test verification**
- **Problem:** Merge broken code, create failing PR
- **Fix:** Always verify tests before offering options

**Open-ended questions**
- **Problem:** "What should I do next?" → ambiguous
- **Fix:** Present exactly 4 structured options

**Automatic worktree cleanup**
- **Problem:** Remove worktree when might need it (Option 2, 3)
- **Fix:** Only cleanup for Options 1 and 4

**No confirmation for discard**
- **Problem:** Accidentally delete work
- **Fix:** Require typed "discard" confirmation

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Proceed with failing tests
- Merge without verifying tests on result
- Delete work without confirmation
- Force-push without explicit request

**Always:**
- Verify tests before offering options
- Present exactly 4 options
- Get typed confirmation for Option 4
- Clean up worktree for Options 1 & 4 only

## Integration

**Called by:**
- **subagent-driven-development** (Step 7) - After all tasks complete
- **executing-plans** (Step 5) - After all batches complete

**Pairs with:**
- **using-git-worktrees** - Cleans up worktree created by that skill

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

Guide completion of development work by presenting clear options and handling chosen workflow.

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## The Process

### Step 1: Verify Tests

**Before presenting options, verify tests pass:**

```bash
# Run project's test suite
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:**
```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]

Cannot proceed with merge/PR until tests pass.
```

Stop. Don't proceed to Step 2.

**If tests pass:** Continue to Step 2.

### Step 2: Determine Base Branch

```bash
# Try common base branches
git merge-base HEAD main 2>/dev/null || git merge-base HEAD master 2>/dev/null
```

Or ask: "This branch split from main - is that correct?"

### Step 3: Present Options

Present exactly these 4 options:

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)
4. Discard this work

Which option?
```

**Don't add explanation** - keep options concise.

### Step 4: Execute Choice

#### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Switch to base branch
git checkout <base-branch>

# Pull latest
git pull

# Merge feature branch
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>

# If tests pass
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

#### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
# Push branch
git push -u origin <feature-branch>

# Create PR
gh pr create --title "<title>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<2-3 bullets of what changed>

## Test Plan
- [ ] <verification steps>
EOF
)"
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

#### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

**Don't cleanup worktree.**

#### Option 4: Discard

**Confirm first:**
```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for exact confirmation.

If confirmed:
```bash
git checkout <base-branch>
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 5)

### Step 5: Cleanup Worktree

**For Options 1, 2, 4:**

Check if in worktree:
```bash
git worktree list | grep $(git branch --show-current)
```

If yes:
```bash
git worktree remove <worktree-path>
```

**For Option 3:** Keep worktree.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | ✓ | - | - | ✓ |
| 2. Create PR | - | ✓ | ✓ | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | ✓ | - |
| 4. Discard | - | - | - | ✓ (force) |

## Common Mistakes

**Skipping test verification**
- **Problem:** Merge broken code, create failing PR
- **Fix:** Always verify tests before offering options

**Open-ended questions**
- **Problem:** "What should I do next?" → ambiguous
- **Fix:** Present exactly 4 structured options

**Automatic worktree cleanup**
- **Problem:** Remove worktree when might need it (Option 2, 3)

name: resolving-merge-conflicts
description: "Use when you need to resolve an in-progress git merge/rebase conflict."
---

1. **See the current state** of the merge/rebase. Check git history, and the conflicting files.

2. **Find the primary sources** for each conflict. Understand deeply why each change was made, and what the original intent was. Read the commit messages, check the PRs, check original issues/tickets.

3. **Resolve each hunk.** Preserve both intents where possible. Where incompatible, pick the one matching the merge's stated goal and note the trade-off. Do **not** invent new behaviour. Always resolve; never `--abort`.

4. Discover the project's **automated checks** and run them — typically typecheck, then tests, then format. Fix anything the merge broke.

5. **Finish the merge/rebase.** Stage everything and commit. If rebasing, continue the rebase process until all commits are rebased.

83:(`gh pr merge --squash <PR>`), unless the user explicitly requests another
84-strategy. Use a clear Conventional Commit title and a final message describing
85-the completed change rather than its intermediate debugging history.
86-
87-A merge request authorizes the merge only after the current PR head passes all
88-required checks and repository review requirements. Recheck the exact head before
89-merging; local checks, earlier green runs and the default strategy do not bypass
90-those gates. Follow the repository's worktree cleanup and branch-preservation
91-rules after integration.

# AI coding reliability guide

Use this guide before implementing or reviewing a change, especially a bug fix,
refactor, merge resolution or optimization. Its purpose is to turn recurring
failure modes into concrete design questions and executable checks. Compiling,
adding a timeout or passing a happy-path test does not establish reliability.

This guide owns the cross-cutting review method and reusable failure patterns.
[Module ownership](module-boundaries.md) owns implementation boundaries;
[architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md), [network contracts](network-design-reference.md)
and feature guides own behavior and resource limits. The
[testing workflow](testing-feedback-loop.md) owns commands, selection and gates.
Link to those owners instead of copying their changing contracts here. When code
and a contract disagree, resolve the intended behavior rather than documenting
the regression as the new rule.

## Use on every change

1. **Locate the owner and consumers.** Read the owning implementation, callers,
   existing tests and relevant guide before adding another helper or state owner.
   Include callbacks, IPC handlers, retries, startup, shutdown and recovery paths;
   an import graph alone cannot reveal all consumers.
2. **State the invariant and select risks.** Describe what must remain true on
   success, failure, cancellation and replacement. Use the table below to select
   applicable rules. A small diff can change lock order or lifetime semantics.
3. **Trace the failure path before editing.** For concurrency work, sketch who
   owns each lock, permit, task and mutable state; what it waits for; and who
   releases it. For a reproducible bug, construct a focused failing regression.
   Record unresolved hypotheses as hypotheses, not confirmed defects.
4. **Implement at the existing boundary.** Preserve authority, durable acceptance,
   compatibility and resource budgets. Recheck invariants after moving work
   outside a guard. Evaluate the proposed fix for new races and deadlocks too.
5. **Verify the changed boundary and report evidence.** Run affected checks and
   required boundary scenarios under the testing workflow. Explain results,
   exclusions and unresolved evidence. Update this guide when the defect exposes
   a reusable failure pattern; follow the maintenance procedure below.

Keep the risk explanation proportional to the change. A documentation edit does
not require a new concurrency test. A changed async callback does require a
lifetime review even when the diff is one line. Put task-specific reasoning and
results in the PR or ignored local evidence, not a new permanent report.

Cross-cutting idle budgets, demand-driven work and accumulation rules belong to
[performance requirements](performance-requirements.md). Apply them alongside the
correctness rules below; a smaller resource chart does not prove preserved recovery.

## Select rules by the changed boundary

| Change or symptom                                                        | Read at least                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Locks, callbacks, synchronous dispatch, UI freezes                       | [R01](#r01-lock-order-and-reentrant-calls), [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure)                |
| Background work, native providers, logout, shutdown or cancellation      | [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions)               |
| Network requests, retries, polling, queues or batches                    | [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R04](#r04-deadlines-cover-the-whole-operation), [R05](#r05-bounded-work-must-also-make-progress)          |
| React effects, IPC reads, dialogs, optimistic updates or mutation status | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R07](#r07-observation-is-not-mutation-ownership), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure) |
| Storage, settings, imports, deletion or recovery                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| IPC/API inputs, files, media or protocol changes                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| Merge resolution, shared helper or dependency changes                    | Revisit the affected callers and all applicable rules; a clean textual merge does not establish compatible ownership or semantics.                    |

These are starting points, not permission to ignore another reachable boundary.
Do not add a global lock, retry loop, timeout or shared abstraction solely to make
the local symptom disappear.

A frozen UI may result from a lock cycle, blocked event thread, starvation, lost
wakeup, unbounded work or stale loading state. Identify the mechanism and the
missing progress condition before selecting a fix; these need different evidence.
# Keeping CI fast and reliable

Treat feedback time, reliability and resource use as maintained requirements.
Every feature, dependency and test can change CI cost, even without a workflow
edit. AI agents and contributors should preserve useful coverage while reducing
unnecessary work, and leave failures easier to reproduce and diagnose.

This guide owns CI maintenance decisions and regression prevention. It does not
introduce another workflow, command catalog or acceptance policy.

| Question                                            | Authoritative owner                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Which tests, commands and CI jobs apply?            | [Testing feedback loop](testing-feedback-loop.md), owning `validation.json` contracts and [workflow definitions](../.github/workflows/) |
| What evidence permits acceptance or release?        | [Quality gates](quality-gates.md) and [version and release lifecycle](updates.md#version-ownership-and-lifecycle)                       |
| Where does an implementation or shared rule belong? | [Module ownership](module-boundaries.md) and [script entry points](../scripts/README.md)                                                |
| Which consumers and documentation need updating?    | [Change alignment checklist](maintenance-checklist.md) and [documentation guidelines](DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md)                      |

Keep tool versions, matrix sizes, deadlines, cache keys and required-check names
in their existing executable owners. Keep run histories and investigation output
in ignored `tmp/` or PR/CI artifacts; durable decisions belong in the owning guide.
For producer/consumer artifact handoffs, pass the successful upload's immutable
artifact ID instead of rediscovering it by name. Keep source, run, attempt and
content-digest validation at the consumer; an artifact ID alone is not acceptance.
Release evidence recording and upload retain their verified-draft prerequisite but run
after final publication failure or cancellation. Keep failure summaries actionable and
source-bound. Nonpublishing branch runs retain workflow-artifact evidence without requiring
a draft. Retained evidence from a failed run is diagnostic; the verified-build owner
still requires successful exact-source jobs/run before authorizing reuse. The existing
release-gates and release-reuse regressions own these producer/consumer boundaries.

## Make the cost of a change explicit

Before adding a suite, fixture, dependency, platform or workflow, identify the
existing owner and the observable failure it must detect. Inspect the affected
plan and consumers through the [validation protocol](testing-feedback-loop.md#validation-stages-and-agent-responsibilities).

Budget hosted job envelopes for cold source builds, scenario execution, evidence
publication and cache cleanup together. Keep build-command and business-scenario
watchdogs independent; successful assertions can still leave an unsuccessful job
when post-actions exceed its envelope. Inspect the timed-out phase and its
measurements before changing a deadline.

Answer four questions in the change when they are material:

- What requirement needs new evidence, and why is existing evidence insufficient?
- Which layer and platform can exercise that requirement faithfully?
- What recurring setup, compilation, execution and artifact cost will it add?
- Can an existing task, fixture or compatible output supply it without weakening
  assertions or introducing another owner for the same rule?

Extend the existing implementation first. Share policy and lifecycle rules where
their meaning is identical; keep feature-specific fixtures local. An abstraction
is useful when it removes duplicated decisions and has clear inputs, outputs and
failure behavior. Avoid both copied shell fragments and a generic CI framework
whose configuration is harder to review than the work it coordinates.

Do not make a full local suite the default for every edit. Use affected feedback
while developing, then complete the applicable boundary and candidate gates.
New tests still need independent assertions; matching the implementation or
increasing a test count does not establish useful coverage.

## Keep workflow policy thin and reject cheap failures locally

Workflows own triggers, permissions, runners, matrices, dependencies and artifact
transport. Scripts own inventory validation, artifact roles, packaging, report
collection and execution policy. Reuse the same CLI locally and in Actions;
extract substantial conditionals and loops into the existing feature owner rather
than copying YAML fragments or introducing another generic orchestration layer.
When moving execution into a script, update every caller and smoke check. Keep
launcher behavior in its owning regression instead of requiring obsolete command
text in YAML. Cross-platform filesystem paths use `fileURLToPath` rather than
`.pathname`; ESM module arguments retain a file URL or relative module specifier
instead of a native Windows absolute path. Exercise each boundary on its platform.
Keep live source/release checks immediately before each publication boundary;
those protect against changed state and are not redundant setup checks.

Consolidate pure checks only when their immutable candidate, scope and inputs are
identical. Health's full-scope Linux portable job owns source standards and Git
index hygiene after frontend dependency setup; documentation scope retains its
independent source gate. Real checker portability fixtures still run on every

# Deploy the marketing site (site/) to GitHub Pages via the Actions deployment flow —
# no gh-pages branch: the page is uploaded as a Pages artifact and published by
# actions/deploy-pages. Requires Settings → Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions".
name: Deploy site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "site/**"
      - "docs/help/**"
      - "tools/help/**"
      - "Cargo.toml"
      - ".github/workflows/pages.yml"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# One deploy at a time; let a newer push supersede an in-flight run.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
name: Mutation Testing

# Pull requests, merge candidates and main pushes verify the pinned runner's
# real caught/survivor/baseline/hang/empty-selection behavior. Broad workspace
# mutation samples run daily or on explicit dispatch, independently of merging.
# Deep samples retain complete baselines, all consumers and strict reports.
on:
  merge_group:
    types: [checks_requested]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 4 * * *' # Daily deep assurance, outside the merge critical path
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: mutants-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}-${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.run_id || 'candidate' }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'merge_group' }}

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  runner-contract:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1
